newsitem.title: USA: Five immigrants die in California freeze.
newsitem.headline: Five immigrants die in California freeze.

text.p: Five illegal immigrants trying to cross treacherous terrain from Mexico into California have died of exposure in freezing temperatures in the past two days, the U.S. Border Patrol said on Wednesday.
"This terrain and this weather is not common in the interior of Mexico. These people were very much unprepared and with little clothing," Salvador Zamora, a Border Patrol spokesman, said.

Three bodies were found on Tuesday in the rugged area east of San Diego. A woman in her late 20s was discovered northeast of Tecate near the border with Mexico and two men, both in their 20s, were found -- one in Pine Valley, the other by a sheriff's deputy in Jamul. Two bodies -- a 17-year-old boy and a 21-year-old woman -- were found near Pine Valley on Monday.
Dozens more illegal immigrants have surrendered to Border Patrol agents to escape the cold, officials said. Many had tried to shield themselves from icy winds with plastic bags.

"The terrain in the East County is very treacherous, mountainous areas with steep canyons, not to mention the weather," Zamora said. "There have been sub-freezing temperatures at night and the last couple of nights we've received some snowfall."

Mexican officials met on Tuesday to get the word out that crossing the border this time of year can be life-threatening. Lourdes Sandoval, spokeswoman for the Mexican Consulate here, said warnings would be posted on Mexico's side of the border from Otay to Tecate and distributed in bus stations and other places where immigrants were likely to congregate.
Zamora said the Border Patrol was also trying to issue warnings through the Mexican media and would issue advisories at its detention centres.
Temperatures were not expected to be as severe over the next few days but a rainstorm was expected to pass through the area before Friday.

Sandoval said 38 immigrants without documents died while trying to make their way through San Diego County last year. But Zamora said many of the deaths last year were attributed to accidents and brush fires and not exposure.
